# NHS Improvement, A Just Culture Guide (deep reference)

**Source:** NHS Improvement (2018). *A Just Culture Guide — Supporting consistent, constructive and fair evaluation of the actions of staff involved in patient safety incidents*. A3 portrait poster, single page. Based on the work of Professor James Reason and the National Patient Safety Agency's Incident Decision Tree. Licence: Open Government Licence v3.0; the poster itself states no licence, and the basis is NHS England's website terms (checked 2026-10-17), which let its published information, logos and photographs excepted, be re-used under the OGL. NHS England now describes the 2018 guide as its own. PDF URL recorded on the source card: https://cpcw.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/19/2018/03/180316-NHSi_just_culture_guide_A3.pdf. The poster prints improvement.nhs.uk in its footer.
**Scope:** open
**Structure:** A single A3 portrait poster comprising: title and subtitle; a three-paragraph preamble framing purpose and use; a four-bullet "Please note" caveat block; five sequential tests (Q1 deliberate harm; Q2 health, with three sub-questions; Q3 foresight, with three sub-questions; Q4 substitution, with three sub-questions; Q5 mitigating circumstances); and seven recommendation end-states distributed across the branches of the tree. The decision tree is the load-bearing apparatus; the preamble carries the principle that "action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate" and frames how to use the guide; the recommendations carry the operational guidance for each branch.
**Citation style:** `(Section, "Subsection")` — for example `(Q3, "Foresight test")` for the foresight test, `(Preamble, paragraph 1)` for the first of the three preamble paragraphs, `(Preamble, "Please note")` for the four caveats. The source is a single page with no page-number anchors; sections are named by the poster's own question numbers (Q1-Q5) and header bars. The poster does not letter its recommendations. This reference labels the seven recommendation end-states A-G, top to bottom, so each can be cited, and cites them unquoted, `(Q1, Recommendation A)`, because the labels are not the poster's words: A is the recommendation on Q1's "Yes" row; B and C sit on Q2's two "Yes" rows (2a; 2b and 2c); D on Q3's "If No to any" row; E on Q4's "If Yes to any" row; F on Q5's "Yes" row; G below the "if No" header bar.
**Coverage:** complete. The single-page poster has been read in full; all four "Please note" caveats, all three preamble paragraphs, all five tests with all sub-questions, and all seven recommendation end-states are represented in the deep reference. No section has been omitted.

## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

The guide's central thesis is that the appropriate response to a member of staff involved in a patient safety incident can and should differ according to the *circumstances in which an error was made* (Preamble, paragraph 3). The poster states that "This guide supports a conversation between managers about whether a staff member involved in a patient safety incident requires specific individual support or intervention to work safely" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 1), and operationalises this through a five-test decision tree. The tests are sequential, with each test gating the next; only one action (or failure to act) is taken through the tree at a time (Preamble, "Please note", bullet 4).

A second load-bearing claim is structural: "action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate - most patient safety issues have deeper causes and require wider action" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 1) [AR]. Two of the tree's end-states restate it: the foresight test (Q3) and the substitution test (Q4) — together accounting for two of the seven end-states — both route to *action singling out the individual is unlikely to be appropriate*, with the patient safety incident investigation pointing to wider actions that may include, but not be limited to, the individual (Q3, Recommendation D; Q4, Recommendation E). Only the deliberate-harm branch (Q1) and the no-mitigating-circumstances branch of Q5 route to management action directed at the individual, and the no-mitigation branch still pairs that action with a directive that "the patient safety incident investigation should indicate the wider actions needed to improve safety for future patients" (Q5, Recommendation G).

A third load-bearing claim is that the guide is a *conversation aid, not a substitute* for either investigation or HR advice (Preamble, "Please note"). Four explicit caveats in the "Please note" block delineate the guide's scope: (i) it is not a replacement for an investigation; only a full investigation can identify the underlying causes; (ii) it can be used at any point of an investigation, but may need to be revisited as more information becomes available; (iii) it does not replace HR advice and should be used in conjunction with organisational policy; (iv) only one action (or failure to act) is taken through the guide at a time, and multiple actions in one incident must be considered separately [AP] (Preamble, "Please note").

A fourth load-bearing claim is that *making the approach explainable* is itself part of a just culture: "An important part of a just culture is being able to explain the approach that will be taken if an incident occurs" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 3). The guide "can be used by all parties to explain how they will respond to incidents" [V], "as a reference point for organisational HR and incident reporting policies, and as a communication tool to help staff, patients and families understand how the appropriate response to a member of staff involved in an incident can and should differ according to the circumstances in which an error was made" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 3). The end the guide serves is dual: "protecting staff from unfair targeting" and protecting patients "by removing the tendency to treat wider patient safety issues as individual issues" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 3).

## Part I: Caveats and framing (Preamble)

### Four caveats on use ("Please note")

The preamble closes with four caveats that set the guide's scope (Preamble, "Please note"):

1. **Not a replacement for investigation.** The guide "is not a replacement for an investigation of a patient safety incident. Only a full investigation can identify the underlying causes that need to be acted on to reduce the risk of future incidents" [V] (Preamble, "Please note", bullet 1).
2. **Usable at any point, open to revisiting.** The guide "can be used at any point of an investigation, but the guide may need to be revisited as more information becomes available" [V] (Preamble, "Please note", bullet 2).
3. **Not a replacement for HR advice.** The guide "does not replace HR advice and should be used in conjunction with organisational policy" [V] (Preamble, "Please note", bullet 3).
4. **One action at a time.** "The guide can only be used to take one action (or failure to act) through the guide at a time. If multiple actions are involved in an incident they must be considered separately" [V] (Preamble, "Please note", bullet 4) [AR]. This caveat enforces a discipline of decomposition: an incident comprising several distinct actions or omissions is not a single trip through the tree but multiple trips, one per action.

### Purpose: a conversation between managers

The guide "supports a conversation between managers about whether a staff member involved in a patient safety incident requires specific individual support or intervention to work safely" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 1) [AR]. The prior is explicit: "Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate - most patient safety issues have deeper causes and require wider action" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 1). The actions of staff involved in an incident should **not** automatically be examined using the guide; the guide is useful when "the investigation of an incident begins to suggest a concern about an individual action" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 2) [AR]. The guide is described as highlighting "important principles that need to be considered before formal management action is directed at an individual staff member" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 2).

### Use as communication tool

Paragraph 3 extends the guide beyond the managers' conversation: it "can be used by all parties to explain how they will respond to incidents" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 3). It also serves as "a reference point for organisational HR and incident reporting policies, and as a communication tool to help staff, patients and families understand how the appropriate response to a member of staff involved in an incident can and should differ according to the circumstances in which an error was made" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 3). The dual purpose is stated: "protecting staff from unfair targeting" and protecting patients "by removing the tendency to treat wider patient safety issues as individual issues" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 3) [AR].

## Part II: The five sequential tests

The decision tree applies five tests in order: deliberate harm, health, foresight, substitution, mitigating circumstances. Each test is gated on the prior: at each test the answer (Yes / No) routes either to a recommendation that exits the tree or to the next test, with the direction varying by test — Q3 proceeds on Yes to all three and exits on any No, and at Q5 both answers exit. Apart from the deliberate-harm exit at Q1, the tree asks about health, protocols, peers, training, supervision and mitigating circumstances before it reaches the other management-action end-state (Recommendation G); the preamble describes the guide as highlighting "important principles that need to be considered before formal management action is directed at an individual staff member" [V] (Preamble, paragraph 2).

### Q1. Deliberate harm test

The first test asks a single question (Q1, "Deliberate harm test"):

**1a.** "Was there any intention to cause harm?" [V] (Q1, "Deliberate harm test").

A Yes answer routes to Recommendation A (deliberate-harm response, see Part III below); a No answer routes to Q2. The deliberate-harm test is the only test in the tree that addresses *intent*; all subsequent tests address conditions and context surrounding an act done without intent to harm [AR].

### Q2. Health test

The second test asks three sub-questions (Q2, "Health test"):

**2a.** "Are there indications of substance abuse?" [V] (Q2, "Health test").
**2b.** "Are there indications of physical ill health?" [V] (Q2, "Health test").
**2c.** "Are there indications of mental ill health?" [V] (Q2, "Health test").

A Yes to 2a routes to Recommendation B (substance-abuse response); a Yes to 2b or 2c routes to Recommendation C (health-issue response); No to all three routes to Q3. The health test is the second filter: Q2 routes these findings to the relevant organisational substance-abuse-at-work or health guidance and wider investigation [AR].

### Q3. Foresight test

The third test asks three sub-questions (Q3, "Foresight test"):

**3a.** "Are there agreed protocols/accepted practice in place that apply to the action/omission in question?" [V] (Q3, "Foresight test").
**3b.** "Were the protocols/accepted practice workable and in routine use?" [V] (Q3, "Foresight test").
**3c.** "Did the individual knowingly depart from these protocols?" [V] (Q3, "Foresight test").

Q3 proceeds to Q4 only on Yes to all three questions: applicable agreed protocols/accepted practice are in place, they were workable and in routine use, and the individual knowingly departed from "these protocols". No to any routes to Recommendation D, which says action singling out the individual is unlikely to be appropriate and that the wider actions indicated by the investigation may include, but not be limited to, the individual [AP].

### Q4. Substitution test

The fourth test asks three sub-questions (Q4, "Substitution test"):

**4a.** "Are there indications that other individuals from the same peer group, with comparable experience and qualifications, would behave in the same way in similar circumstances?" [V] (Q4, "Substitution test").
**4b.** "Was the individual missed out when relevant training was provided to their peer group?" [V] (Q4, "Substitution test").
**4c.** "Did more senior members of the team fail to provide supervision that normally should be provided?" [V] (Q4, "Substitution test").

Yes to any of 4a, 4b, or 4c routes to Recommendation E (not appropriate to single out — substitution branch); No to all three routes to Q5. The substitution test asks whether there are indications that other individuals from the same peer group, with comparable experience and qualifications, would behave in the same way in similar circumstances (4a), whether the individual was missed out when relevant training was provided to their peer group (4b), or whether more senior team members failed to provide supervision that normally should be provided (4c) [AP]. Any Yes routes to Recommendation E: singling out the individual is unlikely to be appropriate, and the wider actions the investigation indicates may include, but not be limited to, the individual [AR].

### Q5. Mitigating circumstances

The fifth and final test asks a single question (Q5, "Mitigating circumstances"):

**5a.** "Were there any significant mitigating circumstances?" [V] (Q5, "Mitigating circumstances").

Yes routes to Recommendation F (action directed at the individual may not be appropriate); No routes to Recommendation G (management action plus wider investigation). Q5 is the residual: only the case that reaches it has cleared the deliberate-harm filter (Q1), the health filter (Q2), the foresight filter (Q3 — Yes to all three questions about applicable agreed protocols/accepted practice, workability and routine use, and knowing departure), and the substitution filter (Q4 — No to the peer-behaviour, missed-training and supervision questions). At that residual point, the final question is whether *significant mitigating circumstances* attach to the case [AR].

## Part III: The seven recommendation end-states

Seven distinct recommendations exit the tree, distributed across the five tests. Two recommendations (D, E) route away from singling out the individual; Recommendation F leaves individual-directed action conditional on the degree of mitigation; two recommendations (A, G) route toward management action directed at the individual; two recommendations route to organisational guidance on substance abuse at work (B) or on health issues affecting work, likely to include occupational health referral (C). Every recommendation pairs its operational guidance with a wider look: A, B and C say wider investigation is still needed; D to G say the patient safety incident investigation should indicate the wider actions needed to improve safety for future patients.

### Recommendation A: deliberate-harm response (exits from Q1 Yes)

> "Follow organisational guidance for appropriate management action. This could involve: contact relevant regulatory bodies, suspension of staff, and referral to police and disciplinary processes. Wider investigation is still needed to understand how and why patients were not protected from the actions of the individual."
>
> [V] (Q1, Recommendation A)

The deliberate-harm path is the only branch the source pairs with potential police referral; regulatory body contact, suspension and disciplinary processes also appear under Recommendation G. Even so, the recommendation closes with "wider investigation is still needed to understand how and why patients were not protected from the actions of the individual" — the system question is not extinguished by the finding of deliberate harm [AR].

### Recommendation B: substance-abuse response (exits from Q2 Yes to 2a)

> "Follow organisational substance abuse at work guidance. Wider investigation is still needed to understand if substance abuse could have been recognised and addressed earlier."
>
> [V] (Q2, Recommendation B)

The response is procedural (organisational substance-abuse-at-work guidance) plus a backward-looking system question: could the substance abuse have been recognised and addressed earlier? [AR]

### Recommendation C: health-issue response (exits from Q2 Yes to 2b or 2c)

> "Follow organisational guidance for health issues affecting work, which is likely to include occupational health referral. Wider investigation is still needed to understand if health issues could have been recognised and addressed earlier."
>
> [V] (Q2, Recommendation C)

Same backward-looking system question, this time applied to physical or mental ill health rather than substance abuse [AR].

### Recommendation D: not appropriate to single out — foresight branch (exits from Q3 No to any)

> "Action singling out the individual is unlikely to be appropriate; the patient safety incident investigation should indicate the wider actions needed to improve safety for future patients. These actions may include, but not be limited to, the individual."
>
> [V] (Q3, Recommendation D)

Under the phrasing "may include, but not be limited to, the individual", the recommendation neither prescribes nor forecloses individual-directed action; the corrective work sits in the wider actions the investigation indicates, with the individual as one possible part of them [AR].

### Recommendation E: not appropriate to single out — substitution branch (exits from Q4 Yes to any)

> "Action singling out the individual is unlikely to be appropriate; the patient safety incident investigation should indicate the wider actions needed to improve safety for future patients. These actions may include, but not be limited to, the individual."
>
> [V] (Q4, Recommendation E)

Recommendations D and E are *textually identical*; they differ in their gating test, not their content. The same qualified response applies at two different exits: No to any of Q3's questions routes to D, and Yes to any of Q4's questions routes to E [AP].

### Recommendation F: mitigating circumstances apply (exits from Q5 Yes)

> "Action directed at the individual may not be appropriate; follow organisational guidance, which is likely to include senior HR advice on what degree of mitigation applies. The patient safety incident investigation should indicate the wider actions needed to improve safety for future patients."
>
> [V] (Q5, Recommendation F)

Recommendations D and E say "is unlikely to be appropriate"; Recommendation F says "may not be appropriate" and directs the reader to organisational guidance, "which is likely to include senior HR advice on what degree of mitigation applies" [V] (Q3, Recommendation D; Q4, Recommendation E; Q5, Recommendation F) [AP].

### Recommendation G: management action plus wider investigation (exits from Q5 No)

> "Follow organisational guidance for appropriate management action. This could involve individual training, performance management, competency assessments, changes to role or increased supervision, and may require relevant regulatory bodies to be contacted, staff suspension and disciplinary processes. The patient safety incident investigation should indicate the wider actions needed to improve safety for future patients."
>
> [V] (Q5, Recommendation G)

Recommendation G is reached on No to Q1; No to all Q2 questions about indications of substance abuse, physical ill health and mental ill health; Yes to all Q3 questions about applicable agreed protocols/accepted practice, workability and routine use, and knowing departure from "these protocols"; No to all Q4 questions about indications of comparable peer behaviour, omission from relevant training provided to the peer group, and failure by more senior team members to provide supervision that normally should be provided; and No to significant mitigating circumstances at Q5 [AP]. The recommendation lists "individual training, performance management, competency assessments, changes to role or increased supervision", and adds that the case "may require relevant regulatory bodies to be contacted, staff suspension and disciplinary processes" [AR]. As with all other recommendations, the wider investigation is preserved as a parallel obligation, not displaced by the individual response.

## Connections the author makes in the text

- **Professor James Reason.** The poster's footer attributes the guide to "the work of Professor James Reason". Reason is named once, in the source's footer; no specific work or concept of Reason's is cited by name (Footer, "Based on the work of Professor James Reason and the National Patient Safety Agency's Incident Decision Tree") [BT].
- **National Patient Safety Agency's Incident Decision Tree.** The footer says the guide is based on the work of the NPSA's Incident Decision Tree. No further detail or citation is provided in the source itself (Footer) [BT].

The poster cites only these two lineages. It does not name any other author, framework, or work.

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

The source does not identify a named opposing author or school. It states that using the guide helps protect patients "by removing the tendency to treat wider patient safety issues as individual issues" (Preamble, paragraph 3) [V]. It also says the guide highlights principles to consider before formal management action is directed at an individual staff member (Preamble, paragraph 2) [AP].

## Citation and source-integrity notes

- **Conversion path.** The source PDF (A3 portrait, single page) is converted with Poppler `pdftotext -raw`, run once per page region: title, preamble, then each decision-tree row's header bar, question column, answer label, recommendation and END HERE marker. The region recipe is recorded in the converted file's header comment and on the source card. The regions together hold the same words as a whole-page run, and the per-row crops keep each answer label ("Yes", "If No to any", "If Yes to any") next to the question and recommendation it joins, so the tree's routing is read from converter output. The converted text adds no headings or labels. Within the Q3 row the converter emits 3b and 3c before 3a; the sub-question numbers carry the order. Image-only content (the NHS Improvement logo, eight supporter logos, a values strapline) is not in the converted text, and no claim here rests on it.

- **Citation style decision.** The single-page poster has no page anchors. Citation style is therefore `(Section, "Subsection")` keyed to the poster's question numbers (Q1-Q5), its header bars, the "Please note" block, or a numbered preamble paragraph. The A-G recommendation labels belong to this reference, not the poster, and are mapped to the poster's rows in the header's citation-style note. They are stable across the deep reference, light reference, and distillations to keep cross-references consistent.

- **Coverage.** Complete. The single-page source has been read in full and every textual element is represented in the deep reference. No section has been omitted; no claim in the deep reference depends on content not present in the converted text.

- **Footer attribution.** The source attributes its lineage to "the work of Professor James Reason and the National Patient Safety Agency's Incident Decision Tree". The deep reference reports this attribution as `[BT]` (borrowed-through) — Reason and the NPSA Incident Decision Tree are named by the source, and any further characterisation of either lineage is outside the scope of this deep reference because it is not stated in the source.

- **Currency (from outside the source).** NHS England's patient-safety pages (https://www.england.nhs.uk/patient-safety/patient-safety-culture/being-fair-tool/, checked 2026-10-17) say NHS England's being fair tool replaces this guide, and that a discovery phase from November 2023 to March 2024 found it no longer fit for purpose. This reference describes the 2018 poster as published, not current NHS England practice. The being fair tool is not in this corpus.
